tldr: Anthropic priced the largest IPO ever at $83 a share, raising $81.3 billion, and starts trading today as ANT.
Trump, Xi and Putin signed a four-point declaration in Shenzhen: nuclear talks, more refined fuel, no mention of Ukraine.
Fed minutes show almost all officials want more hikes; Waller says a half point may be needed to shock people.
The FDA published its rejection letter for Summit's lung-cancer drug: 93% of the trial's events came from China.
Arizona's attorney general opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI over rogue AI agents inside banks.
Nvidia stopped shipping H200 chips to China even though Washington licensed the sales; Beijing will not let them in.
Iran widened its Gulf attacks to a US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain after the Qeshm Island strike.
The FDA approved the first gene-silencing drug for myasthenia gravis, injected four times a year instead of weekly.
Intelligence, homeland security and FBI officials told Congress the cascade of US outages was not an attack.
Trump said Iran is 'looking at gases, looking at bio'; ABC reports the intelligence is unverified and Rubio played it down.

items.headline: Anthropic priced the biggest IPO in history at $83 a share
items.body: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 a share on Wednesday evening, above the $70-to-$78 range it had marketed, and upsized the deal to roughly 980 million shares. That raises about $81.3 billion, the largest stock offering on record, past the roughly $75 billion SpaceX raised in June, at a fully diluted valuation near $1.5 trillion. Trading opens today on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with about 20% of the offering reserved for retail investors. Yahoo Finance put the deal at 925 million shares rather than 980 million.
items.plain: An IPO is the moment a private company sells shares to anyone who wants them, at a price set the night before trading starts. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude assistant, asked for $70 to $78 and got $83, so demand outran its bankers' expectations. The number that matters is the $81.3 billion raised, which is cash for chips and electricity. None of it tells you what the shares are worth: no one has traded them yet.
items.why: The largest pool of outside capital ever raised in one go is now committed to AI model development, which raises the floor on what every competitor must spend to stay in the race.

items.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin signed a four-point declaration after the first three-way summit
items.body: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia met together for the first time on Thursday, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, issuing a four-point declaration after about 90 minutes of talks. It reaffirms that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought," commits the three to a trilateral dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation, backs a more effective United Nations, and pledges to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. There are no warhead reduction targets, and Ukraine does not appear in the text, though Chinese state media said the war was discussed. The document reached the public through Chinese and Russian state media; no US version had been released as of this morning.
items.plain: Three countries hold almost every nuclear weapon on Earth, and until Thursday their leaders had never sat at one table. What they signed is an agreement to talk, not to cut: there is no warhead number in it and no deadline. The fuel clause has the most immediate effect, because Iranian attacks on Gulf shipping have squeezed supply. The telling part is the omission - Ukraine, where Russia is still at war, is not mentioned at all.
items.why: Beijing has always refused US-Russia arms control on the grounds that its arsenal is far smaller, so China signing even a commitment to talk is the concession - and the price was a text that asks nothing of Russia over Ukraine.

items.headline: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect more hikes, and one governor wants a half point
items.body: Minutes of the Federal Reserve's October 27-28 meeting, released Wednesday, show "almost all participants" judged further rate increases would likely be needed to return inflation to 2%, and that two participants raised a half-point move in December. Governor Christopher Waller said the same day the Fed may need to "shock people" with a half point at the December 8-9 meeting; New York Fed President John Williams told Axios, "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action." Futures fully price a quarter point. The rate is 3.75% to 4% after October's 10-2 vote to hold; the dollar hit a 19-month high and gold fell about 3% to a one-year low.
items.plain: The Fed sets the overnight rate banks charge each other, which feeds into mortgages, car loans and credit cards. It is raising that rate because prices are still climbing faster than its 2% target. The minutes, published three weeks after each meeting, show the argument is no longer whether to raise but by how much. Waller's case is partly psychological: a bigger jump is meant to convince people the Fed is serious so they stop expecting prices to keep rising.
items.why: An open split between a Fed governor demanding a half point and the New York Fed president calling that dramatic means December is genuinely unsettled, which is why the dollar and gold moved before any rate changed.

items.headline: The FDA published the letter explaining why it rejected Summit's lung-cancer drug
items.body: The FDA on Wednesday posted the complete response letter, dated November 13, that it sent Summit Therapeutics rejecting ivonescimab for EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer. The agency said effectiveness is not established without a statistically significant improvement in overall survival, which the HARMONi trial did not deliver even though it slowed tumour growth. The letter also notes that 93% of the trial's progression events, 257 of 275, came from patients enrolled in China. Survival figures differ by outlet - one reports a median of 16.8 months versus 14.0 on placebo, BioSpace reports 18.6 versus 14 - and all agree the gap missed statistical significance.
items.plain: Ivonescimab attacks a tumour two ways at once and was the most watched drug of its kind. Its trial showed tumours growing more slowly, called progression-free survival, but did not clearly show patients living longer, called overall survival. The FDA has now said in writing that the first is not enough alone. The geography matters because when nearly all the evidence comes from one country's hospitals, regulators question whether the benefit holds where standard care differs.
items.why: Several of the largest recent biotech deals were built on drugs in this same class, and the FDA has now told all of them that slowing a tumour will not buy an approval without survival data.

items.headline: Arizona opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI over AI agents inside banks
items.body: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday her office has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies over what she called the apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents. She did not name the other companies or the Arizona banks her office contacted, and a criminal investigation does not mean charges will follow. It comes three days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI over alleged AI-driven cyberattacks, and as major US banks block third-party AI agents from customer accounts. OpenAI did not immediately comment and has said it is reinforcing safeguards; the reporting traces to a single Reuters story.
items.plain: An AI agent is a program given a goal and the ability to act on its own - log in somewhere, click through a site, move money - rather than just answer questions. Banking assumes whoever is logged in is a person, and agents break that assumption. Mayes is asking whether turning agents loose on accounts breaks Arizona criminal law, a sharper question than a fine. Note the order: the banks cut agents off first, and prosecutors followed. One news agency has this so far.
items.why: Two state attorneys general moving on the same question in four days suggests agent behaviour is becoming a criminal exposure for the model developer, not just a security problem for the bank.

items.headline: Nvidia stopped shipping H200 chips to China even though Washington approved the sales
items.body: Interim chief executive Colette Kress said on Nvidia's earnings call Wednesday that the company has stopped shipping Hopper-generation AI chips to China despite US approval; the Commerce Department licensed the H200 for China in January. Licensed Hopper sales to China were $2.4 billion last quarter, about 2% of revenue, and the roughly $130 billion forecast for this quarter, plus or minus 3%, excludes China entirely. Nvidia did not say why. Beijing has restricted H200 imports while pushing domestic chips, and Reuters reported about 600,000 of them sitting in Hong Kong awaiting Chinese clearance. Washington still bans the newer Blackwell and Rubin parts.
items.plain: Export controls normally run one way: Washington decides what may be sold, and companies sell it. Here Washington said yes and the chips still are not moving, because the receiving government has to let them in and has not. Beijing wants its own chipmakers to serve that demand, so 600,000 chips sit in a Hong Kong warehouse. The loss is smaller than it sounds - China was about 2% of revenue - which is why Nvidia can write it to zero and still guide to $130 billion.
items.why: The binding constraint on US chip sales to China is now Beijing's import policy rather than Washington's export policy, which strips American export controls of much of their leverage.

items.headline: Iran widened its Gulf attacks to a US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
items.body: Iran's army said Wednesday it had targeted Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, which hosts US forces, with drones, according to state-run Press TV. Kuwait's General Staff said explosions near the base were its air defences intercepting incoming attacks, did not say who launched them, and released no damage figures. Bahrain's military said it intercepted several Iranian aerial attacks and issued shelter alerts, the third interception in a week. Both followed US strikes a day earlier on a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island, which US officials called self-defence.
items.plain: Kuwait and Bahrain are small Gulf states that host large American bases, and both spent this week shooting Iranian drones out of their own skies. That is the escalation: Iran is no longer confining itself to ships and to American assets on Iranian soil. Notice how carefully Kuwait worded it, confirming interceptions without naming Iran - what a government says when it does not want to be pulled in. Iran's mine claims come from Iran alone.
items.why: Each strike on a Gulf host state pulls Kuwait and Bahrain closer to being parties to the war rather than bystanders, and their airspace sits directly over the lane most of the world's seaborne oil passes through.

items.headline: The FDA approved the first gene-silencing drug for myasthenia gravis, dosed four times a year
items.body: The FDA approved Regeneron's Livsayis, or cemdisiran, for adults with generalised myasthenia gravis who test positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. It is the first small interfering RNA therapy cleared for the disease and the only approved gMG treatment given by subcutaneous injection every 12 weeks. In the Phase 3 NIMBLE trial, cemdisiran patients improved 4.2 points on the QMG muscle-strength scale versus 1.5 on placebo, and 48.4% gained at least 5 points versus 19%; the trial randomised 64 patients to cemdisiran, 67 to a combination with pozelimab and 59 to placebo, and was published in The Lancet. It is the second gMG approval this week, after AstraZeneca's gefurulimab on Monday.
items.plain: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the signal between nerve and muscle, so patients lose strength in the eyes, throat and limbs and tire within minutes. Existing drugs of this type are infusions or injections every week or two - a lifetime of appointments. Cemdisiran silences the gene that makes the harmful immune protein instead of mopping the protein up afterwards, and that silencing lasts about three months. Four injections a year rather than roughly fifty is the change patients feel.
items.why: Dosing frequency, not efficacy, usually decides whether chronic patients stay on treatment, so a quarterly injection reshapes a crowded disease more than another incremental efficacy gain would.

items.headline: Intelligence and FBI officials told Congress the wave of US outages was not an attack
items.body: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that the recent failures were "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes" and "not a coordinated or state sponsored attack." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, "We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia said bureau cyber specialists had examined the incidents from the start. Clayton said the evidence points toward legitimate efforts to secure systems rather than malicious activity, while acknowledging the timing raised concerns. The outages hit banks, airlines and Apple services and included a five-hour FAA ground stop.
items.plain: Over the past week, systems with nothing to do with each other failed in quick succession: bank payments, air traffic computers, Apple services. The obvious suspicion was an attack. The officials who would know say it was routine maintenance and security updates going wrong, several times, at several companies. That is less frightening and more uncomfortable, because an attacker can be deterred and ordinary fragility cannot. The hearing did not explain why so many independent systems break the same way at once.
items.why: If unconnected maintenance can take down banking and air travel in one week, the vulnerability is structural concentration in a few shared providers, which no counter-threat agency is built to fix.

items.headline: Trump said Iran is 'looking at gases, looking at bio'; his own secretary of state played it down
items.body: Asked by Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich at the APEC summit in Shenzhen about reports of an Iranian plot against Washington, Trump said Iran is "looking at gases, looking at bio." He offered no evidence, said he did not think Iran would attack Washington, and added, "If it does happen, we wipe them out." The underlying report, published by CNN on November 16, cited seven US officials describing intelligence that Iran had drawn up plans to target senior administration officials with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon. Sources told ABC News that intelligence has not been verified, that officials were divided on it, and that it was characterised as Tehran giving itself options rather than an imminent threat. Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved to play the warning down, and Iran's UN mission called the allegations fabricated.
items.plain: A dirty bomb is conventional explosive packed with radioactive material: it contaminates an area rather than levelling it. US intelligence picked up signs Iran had drawn up such plans, and officials reading the same material disagreed about how much to believe. That is normal - intelligence arrives in fragments and gets graded for confidence before anyone acts. Here the president skipped the grading in public, turning a disputed report into a flat claim about chemical and biological weapons, and his own secretary of state then walked it back.
items.why: Pre-war claims about unconventional weapons are the one category of presidential statement that cannot be withdrawn, and the administration is now publicly split over whether its own intelligence supports this one.
